utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There is nothing I think we should pay attention to before we resume the cross-examination of the witness. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time for the following. It's about a remaining issue from the testimony of Dragic Gojkovic. During his testimony on the 12th of August of this year, D1184 was marked for identification pending the provision of its English translation. This is to be found at transcript pages 37667 to -669. On the 14th of October, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution via an e-mail that it had received a CLSS translation of D1184 bearing doc ID 1D26-1428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As usual, 48 hours are given to express any concerns about it, but the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translation to D1184 and admits it into evidence. Again, 48 hours to revisit the matter if need be. Good morning, Mr. Poparic. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Apparently not. Could the audio be checked for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was caused by my speed of speech. I'm aware of that and I'll try to improve. Good morning, Mr. Poparic. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Just one preliminary --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One preliminary matter, Your Honours, and it's with respect to some video-clips that we viewed last week during Mr. Poparic's examination-in-chief, and they are from 65 ter number 1D05925, which has the ERN number V000-2817, beginning at time code 1:51:35. Now, last week Your Honours expressed interest in having frame-by-frame exposures of parts of those clips which we had seen in court. And actually because we had a three-day weekend, I was able to secure those frame-by-frame stills which we now have available to you under 65 ter number 33365 described as 46 still frames from 65 ter number 1D05925. Now, I have -- I don't propose to deal with them with the witness, subject to any direction Your Honours might have. It's just by way of being responsive to Your Honours' request. And unless there is an objection, I would -- and keeping in mind we still haven't dealt with the actual videos, but I would propose to tender these frame stills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Lukic, I think these were -- it was your examination-in-chief which triggered all that, and that's about the -- Ms. Edgerton, that's about the either incoming or outgoing projectiles next to a window and not next to a window. That's the series where you're talking about. Mr. Lukic, do you have any interest in, well, having it available in such a way that the Chamber can look at it still by still? Because then if it's available, you might -- I think it was your line of questioning that we would then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not -- we would not object, of course, but we did our homework as well, so I would like to compare. Maybe we can even add one to each other and to have as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I noticed that at least one of the stills is reproduced in the report by the witness. Then we leave it. We put it on hold for the time being, but the Chamber certainly is interested to have those stills available which allow for a -- perhaps for a better analysis of what exactly can be seen in this video. We'll leave it for a while to you, and could we say that by the end of the testimony of this witness that you would revisit the matter. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And just the final thing for everyone. We've now released a public redacted version of P1130, which was of course admitted under seal. And that public redacted version has the 65 ter number 28541B. So if we could use that, unless otherwise indicated, I think that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can use it, but as always, public redacted versions will not be admitted into evidence. They are just for use in court and may be brought to the attention of the public by other means but not as a part of the evidence before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. It was just to avoid going in and out of private session wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, before we go back to where we left off on Thursday, I'd like to invite you to have a look at paragraph 10 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies for the delay. I had omitted the page numbers, but in English it appears at page 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you should give the 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is the unredacted version, I think. But you wanted to use the redacted -- public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, I'm referring to Mr. Poparic's report. But when I described a public redacted version, that is Mr. Van der Weijden's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just your indulgence for a moment and apologies -- oh, thank you to my friend for finding the paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So here in paragraph 10, the very first line, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have the English version --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see the very first line of paragraph 10 reads: "According to the reports available to us, the victims were predominantly civilian." Now, in this sentence you are talking about the victims of sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You can -- thank you for answering my question. I just want to move on. Now, in terms of the identification of those victims as civilians, you referred to a document that's got the Defence 65 ter number 1D05640. And if we could have a look at that, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about it. Now, this isn't translated, and I think that for the -- oh, parts of it are translated. Wonderful. And this document you know is -- is a document in two parts; right? The first 40-some odd pages is -- actually, the first 44 pages is part of an index to a list of sniping casualties in Bosnian-held Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this list - and we could just flip over one page in B/C/S - this list, you know from reviewing it, also refers to supporting material; right? So for each incident it lists persons killed or wounded by surname and first name, date of birth, sometimes where they have it location of the incident, and underlying each name there is a range of supporting material; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the English version doesn't seem to accord with the B/C/S one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. And it's not my translation. I would propose to -- this is a Defence-uploaded document I'm referring to, so perhaps in the interests of accuracy we could just deal with the B/C/S version for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, from reviewing this document, you would agree with me that the range of supporting material for each incident includes things from medical records; right? It includes medical records.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, and --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sometimes it includes death notices; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is different information. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it's not the same for each and every case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So just let me go through the range, if you don't mind. Sometimes it includes official police notes, investigative material; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And sometimes the supporting material refers to statements of victims or survivors; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that there are statements, but if that's what you're saying, I will agree with you. But I'm not quite sure about statements. It's possible that there are statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And sometimes the lists of supporting material include reference to photographs and forensic reports, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I found that. But we can check.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll give you a chance to do that, I think, later on. Now, you relied on this document. You cite to it actually in your footnotes 23, 71, 241 and 242, 244, 299, and 600 as the basis for a range of assertions. So I just want to ask you, since you relied so heavily on the document, a couple more questions about the contents. Just dealing with the first 45 pages that would have -- the ERN number 0097-0276 to 0318. Now, that's a list of sniping victims from September to December 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you acknowledge, by the way, that this material is incomplete? You've skipped over all of 1993, haven't you? There is no material for 1993 in this list at all.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I skipped anything. I didn't have it available. I think that I've already said that, that there wasn't anything for 1993, and I've already said that I analysed what it was that I had available.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So what you analysed from September to December 1992 shows 258 people wounded as a result of sniping; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 256 according to my report. Well, there is a difference of two. Well, it doesn't really matter, does it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, actually it does matter. That's why we're dealing with these figures. And we've counted 87 killed from September to December 1992, this range of documents.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my report, 99.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this list includes children, you've indicated that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Includes all who were registered as sniping victims; that is to say, children, women, men, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you found among that the victim -- the victim of Scheduled Incident F-1 who you referred to in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I listened well to him, I think he mentioned the name of the victim of F-1, that's what I heard directly. Is that what did, Witness? Anisa Pita?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anisa Pita, 13th of December, 1992. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also found in that list a number of people with the date of birth before 1930, didn't you? People who were over the age of 60 at the time they were killed or wounded; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to page 46 -- either 45 or 46 of this 65 ter number. It's part of a different file index dealing with victims of sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo from January to August 1994. And it's correct, isn't it, that this different index breaks down the victims month by month; right? You can look at the screen and you can see the document I'm talking about in front of you. It's correct that they breakdown the lists of victims killed and wounded by sniping month by month; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you found in there victims of scheduled sniping incidents that you dealt with in your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this 65 ter number, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D05640 receives Exhibit Number P7594.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Poparic, over the course of your cross-examination I'd like to know, would you be prepared to have a look at the list from 1993 which was missing from the index that you offered and answer some questions about it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that list until now. I can take a look. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll make sure to have a copy of it prepared for you and delivered to you and allow you enough time to be able to review it. But for now I want to get back to some of the incidents that we were talking about before we left off on Thursday, and I want to stay, please, with F-5. That's the incident in Brijesce Brdo. Now, in respect of that incident you mention a tank and you mentioned it in a paragraph 89, which is at page 126 in English and 124 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at Mr. Poparic's report so he can see those pages, that reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you say here that Ms. Kundo did concede, however, that there was a BH army tank by the church some 500 metres above her house, but she didn't know if the tank had ever fired. And your comment is that the presence of the tank in itself isn't directly linked to the incident but it indicates that there were troops in the Brijesce Brdo area -- pardon me, on Brijesce Brdo whose members could have been the target of attack in this case. Now, you mentioned this very -- this -- actually, you had the identical paragraph in your Karadzic report, so we talked about it, if you'll remember, in your Karadzic testimony. Do you remember that at that time I pointed out to you that you had omitted to mention that Mrs. Kundo actually testified that she didn't even know what year the tank was there, that it could have been 1993 or 1994? Do you remember that I pointed that out to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said, but I did not find that piece of information that she said that; that is, the tank was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember that I also pointed out to you that the tank was only -- that she testified that the tank was only there on that site for seven days sometime within that two-year period? Do you remember that I pointed that out to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the tank wasn't there only seven days. Mr. Brennskag testified about that, a military observer who saw that tank from the observation post number 4 at Vitkovac. So the tank was probably there for a long period of time. That is my opinion. Which does not mean that Ms. Kundo had to know about it. Maybe she didn't. But according to the military observer's statements, the tank was there for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, when I pointed this out to you in the Karadzic case, you said: "It's not for us to say when this happened. We just mentioned that a tank was there." You didn't say anything at that time about not finding that information, so are you changing your evidence now?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing my evidence. I just didn't mention it there. I can't always answer exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, the effect of not mentioning it -- actually, the effect of your selective excerpting might create the impression that Mrs. Kundo said that the tank was there at the time of the incident. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. If she said it wasn't there, it wasn't there according to her, which again doesn't mean that it wasn't. She knows that it wasn't there in a period of seven days, whereas the military observers were there for a much longer time. That's the extent to which she knows the situation. If she claims it wasn't there on that day, then that's her evidence. But that a tank was prevent in that area is a fact. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, let's just get back to her evidence. You're now arguing with me about what her evidence might be and the weight of it. The fact is you knew about this omission, the omission is significant because it goes to influence your argument as to military targets or potential military targets in the area, and you left that information out again; right? That's the fact.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that Mrs. Kundo didn't know the exact period, that's true. But I'm telling you her knowledge does not coincide with the knowledge of the military observers. That's why her evidence doesn't rule out the possibility that the tank was there within a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- could I just ask you where exactly is the -- because we don't have the name of the military observer. Where is that to be found exactly in your report, the observation by the military observer about the presence of a tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mention it in the report, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in his statement it is there. Brennskag is the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in the report. In the report you present it as if there would have been a tank. Any discussion about when that tank was there, that there is apparently evidence which may have to be reconciled is not something you mentioned. You just leave it to the suggestion that the tank would have been there most likely at that point in time. That's the impression you give us. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. If there is other information which confirms that, I have nothing against it. This is the knowledge that I had as to what Mrs. Kundo stated. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from the basic question of whether it's for you to assess the probative value of one piece of evidence against another piece of evidence, apart from that basic question, wouldn't you think that it would be appropriate, if you do it, to present all the elements so that it is transparent on which information your conclusions are drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly it would be a good idea to present as much evidence as possible. I only looked at her evidence and didn't go into it deeply. I saw that there was mention of a tank, but there were probably troops as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Probability, I -- now, if this was highlighted in the Karadzic case, don't you think that it would have been appropriate, where apparently there was a problem in relation to all this or at least it was discussed, then at least in your new report to give more information, more detailed information where you knew that it had caught the attention that there was evidence which might not be fully consistent in every respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's true that I omitted that. But even then I didn't claim that it was very important from my point of view. I mentioned it in passing. I did not draw a single conclusion as to how the incident happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you suggested that those -- that tank and those troops may have been the target of the attack in this case. That's a suggestion which goes in one direction. You have left out any suggestion going into the direction that they perhaps probably would not have been there and therefore could not explain it. You agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but I made a suggestion. It's not a claim that it's the cause of the incident. That's one. And two, I certainly did not have enough information in order to elaborate on whether it was there at that particular moment or not. I only suggested that there was mention about that tank, but I did not have enough information. There could be other witnesses and other evidence that is not available to me, so I mentioned it just in passing. It's not a basis on which I am relying in this case. I said I don't have the necessary elements, from the point of view of my profession, to make any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You considered to make these loose suggestions relying on part of a witness testimony only, you find that in line with your professional expert duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand you. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question is whether you consider it appropriate for an expert in your professional field to make loose suggestions which are based only on part of what a witness said and leave out other parts of what the witness said which might go in a different direction. You find that appropriate for an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when I was writing this, that's the information that I had. I did not mention simply what was pointed out to me by the Prosecutor, but there was no intention to misrepresent anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For your report in the Mladic case, you knew that there was other information because you learned that during the Karadzic testimony, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just omitted to add it. I forgot. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I don't attach great importance to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you just told us or referred to Brennskag's evidence about the tank, you omitted to say that Brennskag never saw the tank firing, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention Brennskag in my report at all precisely because I did not attach importance to that tank. Yes, it's true that Brennskag said that. I just said that he was aware of that tank. I didn't quote all of his evidence, and he did say, among other things, that he never saw the tank firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Brennskag's statement, by the way, Your Honours, is P992, and the evidence about the tank is in paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in any case, whether or not a tank was in the area at whatever time and whether or not it was even operational doesn't mean that you can snipe at civilians engaged in civilian activities, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that anywhere. Of course that's no reason to target civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to go on to the incident in your report that's described as F-6, and you find it in the section beginning at English page 132 and B/C/S page 130, paragraphs 96 to 113. Now, the allegation in this incident is that on the 6th of January, 1994, Sanija Dzevlan, a 32-year-old woman, was shot and wounded in her buttocks while she was riding a bicycle across a bridge on Nikola Demonja Street in Dobrinja. Now, first of all you agree that this happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also agree that there is a clear, unstructured line of sight between the place of the incident and the Orthodox church in Veljine; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you talked about this incident in your Karadzic testimony and told the Court at that time, and you've made the same claim here, that, in your opinion, this incident took place at around 4.30 p.m., and that was on the basis that the victim in this case went to visit her mother in the hospital in Dobrinja and stayed on past normal visiting hours. And you say that in this report at paragraph 99, English page 137, and pages 133 and 134 in B/C/S. And then you proceeded to develop an argument on visibility from the alleged origin of fire based in part on the time estimate I've just outlined to you, but you know in fact that Sanija Dzevlan's mother wasn't even in the hospital. She didn't go there to visit her. She went there to get medicine. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well because it was a big debate during my testimony in the Karadzic case. She stated what I cited here and it's in the transcript. Even the Prosecutor recalled that she had been calling on her mother. I did not analyse the incident only from the point of view of that time-frame. I used two versions. And the conclusion was based not only on visibility but also on the ballistic analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's just focus on your assertion about her visiting her mother. She never said she was visiting her mother. Mr. Poparic, you've analysed that testimony. It was the Prosecutor who said it in error. And if you want, we could even look at that, but I'm sure you remember that point. And then I pointed out to you in your Karadzic testimony that the victim specifically explained this during her testimony in the Galic case. And then before she concluded her Galic testimony -- and actually, let's have a look at her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 32755 in e-court, please. And if we could go to e-court page 45, I think. This is a transcript -- a copy of the transcript of testimony of Sanija Dzevlan on 12 February 2002 in the Galic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps it's easier if we just go over to the immediately preceding page so we can see the whole paragraph and who's speaking. So we would need 3555.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you see at the bottom of page 3555 His Honour Judge El Mahdi has a few questions, and he says at line 23: "First of all, you said that you were returning from a visit to your mother at the hospital, and I was able to understand that in reply to another question, you said that you left to look for medicines. I don't know exactly whether I understood properly or misunderstood what you said. Why did you, in fact, go out?" And she responded: "My mother was sick at home. I went to the hospital to fetch medicines and to bring those medicines back [sic] to her." You looked at her Galic testimony because you have a footnote to it in your report. You knew this. You knew that she had corrected any misunderstanding in response to a question by the Trial Chamber, but in this report you haven't changed a thing about what -- about your assertion as to what she was doing at the hospital; right? You haven't changed a thing.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement she said that after lunch she went to the hospital to see her mother, and she testified here exactly the same as I quoted. It's true that she went. And for me that was the only thing I had in mind. I didn't judge on whether she stated accurately what she was doing, whether she was going to visit. But I estimated if she was going to visit, then it was around 4.00 p.m., and I said in my report what kind of visibility is expected at that time. So I didn't judge her testimony from the point of view of whether it is accurate or not. I took into account two possibilities: Whether it was during daylight or at dusk, twilight. And that's what I put in my report. And the final conclusion was not even based on this but on the ballistic analysis of the bullet. That's why I didn't go into any analysis of her statements, because for me there are two statements --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Stop.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that it was earlier or that it was later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Stop. When I pointed all this out to you in the Karadzic testimony, you conceded: "Perhaps I missed that detail." And that's in your Karadzic evidence at 39166 lines 17 to 20. And you still haven't corrected it; right? You still haven't corrected it; right? Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not correct it and I explained why. I wasn't dealing with whether she was giving correct or incorrect evidence. I took into account two possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've answered the question. So the effect of picking this time that's not supported by the evidence, picking this time that had her in hospital as long as possible could put her on the bridge where she was shot as late as possible, which would influence any argument you might make on her visibility from the alleged firing position. That was the effect of your excerpting; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I repeat. For me in this case --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, you don't --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were two pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You don't need to repeat anything. I want to go on to another incident just for the moment, and I'm going to stay with, actually, Dobrinja for a moment. Now, in respect of the incident, which is F-3 in your report, which is at English page 85 and B/C/S page 99, and beginning at paragraph 45, you said that the time of the incident is in dispute, you said that in your testimony here, and pointed out that according to the police report the incident took place between 7.00 and 7.30 p.m. And a lady neighbour, Sadija Sahinovic who was with Zametica claimed -- I'll tell you what your testimony is. It was at 40416, lines 19 to 25. You said Sahinovic said that during her testimony, when it was just about to get dark. This matches the police report but later on she corrected what she had said. Then there is her death certificate at a different to time and so on. Now, just with respect to the police report and Sahinovic, what I noticed you didn't mention in your testimony or in your report -- actually, no, let's stick with your report. What I noticed you didn't mention in your report was that in the Galic trial, Sahinovic was shown the report, which is P973, page 2, she was shown it, the report that you cite to that has the time of death between 7.00 and 7.30, and she specifically noted that the time in it was wrong. And she specifically said that she and the victim went to the river between 2.00 and 3.00. That's what she said. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. However, this is almost the same case as the previous one you mentioned. I had two times here, and I didn't go into all the evidence, judging what is accurate or not. I assume that both are correct and I analysed the case in that way. So when one determines what is correct, then it's easy to reject the other possibility. For me there were two times: One given in the police report, one given in witness testimony. I analysed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the two. What is true, I don't know. It was not up to me to judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you are recorded as having said: "I assume that both are correct ..." Is that what you said or did you say: "I assume that both are not correct"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not the point of my answer. For me, there are two given times: One from the police, one from the witness. I don't go into which one is correct, but I analysed the case using these two times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I now better understand what you meant by "for me both are correct." Of course they couldn't be both correct, but for your line of thinking you assumed that both are correct. Yes. Which gives two different scenarios.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's a matter of interpretation. Yes, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is -- or, actually, tell me if I have this correct. What you're saying is you knew that Sahinovic had specifically corrected the time of the police report. You knew that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about two times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, witness explained how he worked and why he worked the way he did. If the Prosecution has the witness who claimed two facts about the same event, I don't think that it's wrong on the expert's side to analyse both of them. So if they think that he shouldn't have analysed both scenarios, we object to that and this line of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do you deny the witness to analyse both scenarios?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, no, of course not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that's -- then we understand your line of questioning not attacking the witness on that point but that you are seeking other evidence. Therefore, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, the point is the other scenario isn't mentioned in your report. You don't mention Sahinovic's specific correction in your report; right? You're just telling us about it now.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was using two times. That's the point. This correction is contained in the two times that I am using: 1400 hours and 1430, or 1900 hours, 1930. I didn't take into account the testimony of Mrs. Sahinovic as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was just having a look at my watch, Your Honour. I think we might be one minute away from break time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. The witness may follow the usher. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I would like to briefly pay attention to a remaining issue from the testimony of John Russell. On the 7th of September of this year during his testimony, D1221, a report on crater analysis with the witness's handwritten comments on it, was marked for identification pending an upload of a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the 21st of October, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution via an e-mail that a translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 1D26-2871. The Prosecution advised the next day that it did not object to the translation, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translation to D1221 and admits D1221 into evidence. Apologies, Mr. Poparic, for dealing with administrative matters when you entered the courtroom. Ms. Edgerton will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic, am I correct in assuming that before filing at least the corrigendum to your report you checked your citations? You reviewed your report and checked your citations for accuracy?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot discern what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did my best to check whether there were any mistakes. I cannot say whether I was successful. I hope I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. Then maybe you can answer my questions about a couple that jumped out. One is in respect of Incident F-2 in your report, and you'll find the section related to that incident beginning at, I think, page 83 and English page 80. And the allegation there is that on 17 April 1993, a 9-year-old girl was shot and wounded in the back while playing in the front garden of her house in Sedrenik. So you agree this happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in your report for this case at paragraph 37 - and that's on, as I said, English page 80, B/C/S page 83 - you said she was facing the street at the moment she was shot, and you said the same thing in your Karadzic report. Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I want you to just have a look at the footnote for that citation. All right? So you footnoted your citation to her location to her transcript in her testimony in the Galic case. Now, in the Karadzic case, during that trial we talked about this as well. And I told you that I had a look at the transcript page that you had cited and found that there wasn't any reference on that page or actually anywhere in her testimony that she was facing the street, but in fact she said she was facing Spicasta Stijena at the moment she was shot. Do you remember my telling you that and do you remember confirming that that was correct? She wasn't facing the street, she was facing Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I do not remember that you said that to me, but she was facing the street, and in that position Mr. Barry Hogan filmed it, and now the only debate is whether that direction is the direction of Spicasta Stijena or not. However, she was in that position facing the street a bit. Now, she was certainly facing the street. That's the way she showed it herself. However, I do have to say that the street cannot be seen very clearly because there are some houses in between. But seen from the air, she was facing the street. Now, whether she was facing --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Spicasta Stijena or not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and let's go to your testimony in Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32790, please. If we could go to e-court page 60, please, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Here's where we talked about this. Starting at line 2, you said, and I put this to you: "... you said in your analysis of this incident that the victim who was shot was kneeling down with her back turned towards the house and ... was facing the street." And further in that paragraph is what I just summarised to you about what her Galic testimony actually said. And I noted that: "... she clarified at transcript pages 4042 to 4047, that she was facing spiky rock which is Spicasta Stijena at the moment she was shot." And then you said at line 12: "That's it. If she was turned in the direction of Spicasta Stijena, it is understood that she was looking in that direction." Are you changing your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not. I said a moment ago her back was turned to the back and she was facing the street, and in that direction as she was watching, she could have been watching Spicasta Stijena, Grdonj, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no basic difference there. If the reference is not correct, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Stop. You answered my question. Let's go on to another citation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd like to do this in private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, I want to go from here to a neighbourhood that you deal with in your report and four sniping incidents that are alleged to have taken place in that neighbourhood, and it's Sedrenik. And as part of your analysis, you made some general observations about the neighbourhood and referenced in particular a witness by the name of Nedzib Djozo. And that's at paragraph 16, English page 58, and B/C/S page 61. And you said there: "Some of the witnesses testified that the RS Army had been sniping at civilians in contrast to the evidence of Nedzib Djozo who testified that many citizens of Sarajevo, including himself, would come to the woods beneath Spicasta Stijena to cut trees. That part of the woods was cleared of trees, according to Djozo, and nobody was targeted there, although it was close to Spicasta Stijena." Are you actually trying to tell us that Djozo's evidence -- that the crux of Djozo's evidence is that nobody sniped at civilians in Sedrenik from Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for this part of Djozo's testimony, I mention it in relation to this forest, and you can see that in image 26, that is a bit above this number 3 as it is marked here. He himself said that he came there and cut firewood and all of those trees were cut down. There is only young trees there now. And he did not say that somebody fell victim there. It was below Spicasta Stijena. I'm just saying -- I'm just speaking about that area. So I mean they were coming there at night, cutting trees, and the Army of Republika Srpska did not open fire at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just we need the next page in B/C/S. This is wrong page -- wrong citation, so that the witness can follow what he was asked about. He was asked about the first paragraph above the picture on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Djozo when he talked about tree cutting wasn't talking about woods beneath Spicasta Stijena at all. He was talking about Sedam Suma, Seven Forests. And Sedam Suma isn't between or isn't beneath Spicasta Stijena at all, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sedam Suma? Is it Sedam Suma, Pet Suma, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at his testimony in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 1D00443. You could go over to page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, look, on page 9, lines -- starting at line 12, he lays out the description of the neighbourhood and the immediate surroundings, and he looks at a photograph -- and we'll come to the photograph in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And he says, starting at line 18 and referring to the photograph: "These houses are parts of Sedrenik, which lies to the right of Spicasta Stijena. Here we see two elevations and the road that goes around to Spicasta Stijena ... there is no forest. It was cut down during the war. This area was known as 'Seven Forests,' but during the war people in the city needed firewood, and they came here and cut down trees and took them to Sarajevo to use as firewood."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, let's go, please, to 65 ter number 23143.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is my learned friend claiming that in this part of the statement Mr. Djozo is not talking about area in between Spicasta Stijena and Sedrenik? Is that the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Poparic seemed to need some help as to what area Mr. Djozo was discussing as to where the firewood was chopped down and he couldn't remember if it was Seven Forests or Five Forests. And I was simply showing him the testimony of Mr. Djozo that he referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think Mr. Lukic is interested to know -- to find out and that the Chamber should know where Seven Forests is in relation to Spicasta Stijena, Sedrenik, and he has an opportunity to further elaborate that. But if you could already deal with it, since you make quite a bit of -- you put quite some importance on Seven Forests not to be what the other witnesses are talking about. Perhaps to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter number 23143, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is the picture that Mr. Djozo marked in his Karadzic testimony, and that happened at pages 9590 to 9591 of the document we just looked at, e-court pages 38 to 39. He marked at number 1 the peak of Grdonj. He marked --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, we have the different -- we have to go to transcript that. That's how we deal with these markings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton has to show us first the transcript and then the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what has to be shown first or second is -- apparently there is some dispute about what the marking means. If there is dispute about that, Ms. Edgerton, I think it would be appropriate to verify that in order to not waste time. And perhaps we could have English transcript on the one hand side and then perhaps the picture on the other, which would allow us to follow both the words spoken and the markings made.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: His -- this transcript is at 1D05713, e-court pages 38 and 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if you look here, Dr. Karadzic asks Mr. Djozo to mark the peak of Grdonj at line 10. Mr. Djozo, at lines 12 to 13, marks Grdonj with an arrow from the sky pointing down to the peak and puts the number 1 next to it and points out that there is relay towers at lines 15 to 16 on Grdonj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The reference to the relay towers is contained in the question not in the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, pardon me. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then Dr. Karadzic asks whether he can mark Spicasta Stijena, and that's at line 19. And he then responds by drawing a line where Spicasta Stijena is and a number 2. They then deal with Pasino Brdo or Streliste which is "located to the right, behind this part where you can see that the trees are cut, Pasino Brdo is behind this ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "... area." And Dr. Karadzic said: We're going to deal with that later. And he asks him to mark the area where the trees were cut during the war. And Mr. Djozo indicates that with a dotted line and marks it with a number 3 at Dr. Karadzic's request. And that's at line 6. And he asks -- Dr. Karadzic asks: "So this clearing was made during the war. People cut the trees down in order to have wood for heating; is that correct?" "Yes," is the response. And then he marks Sedrenik as his last item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A reference to "4" is missing here but it's the last marking. At least I don't see it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't see it at this moment either, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's uncertain, but at least there is a marking and there is a marking with a number 4 attached to it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The woods where trees were cut are not beneath Spicasta Stijena as you said in your report and that's according to the evidence of the witness you cited; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forest that I mentioned in the report that was marked by Mr. Djozo is located below Spicasta Stijena, a little bit to the left. And that's clearly seen on this picture number 26. The whole hill is under a young forest. You were there, you saw it. The trees had been cut down and now the forest is growing again. When you see the picture, you see very clearly that young forest. It's just a little below Spicasta Stijena but within the range of the weapons. It's that forest and I didn't make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have this photograph tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, are you going to also tender this portion of the testimony just to see the markings?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23143 receives Exhibit Number P7595.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And pages 38 and 39 which reflect Djozo's evidence about these markings that Your Honours have been looking at as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Pages 83 -- sorry, 38 and 39 of document 1D5713 receives Exhibit Number P7596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it should be -- that excerpt is not specifically downloaded, therefore we'll MFI it. And you'll take care, Ms. Edgerton, that the portion we need will be given a 65 ter number. Witness, could I just ... you say: I'm sure this is where the trees were cut. Now, we saw that the witness marked the area where trees were cut with a dotted line with number 3, which is not below Spicasta Stijena. So therefore, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the difference in altitude, and it's a bit to the left. There is a road here. I'm looking at photograph 26 in my report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that -- what you may have presented, but you are telling us what Mr. Djozo testified. And if I look at the markings made by Mr. Djozo, I see that 2, that is, marked as Spicasta Stijena, and number 3, the area where the trees are cut, that area 3 is not below area 2. Therefore, when you say, well, that's how it was, you are referring to his testimony, and I have some difficulties in understanding how the dotted line with the 3 fits under 2, rather than to the right of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at this arrow number 3, a bit to the left of it is the top of this hill, and this dotted line is going to the left towards Spicasta Stijena downhill --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I do not see -- but perhaps I'm wrong, I do not see the dotted line going any further than a little bit to the right of where number 4 is marked. So is it that you say that is how it should have been, or is it that you say I'm missing something in the marking in this photograph? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't stretch all the way to number 4. The dots go from the top of this hill marked 3, and you see a curve, that's a slope. It can clearly be seen from Spicasta Stijena. And that's all covered by the forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what I'm still unable to see is how the area marked by the dotted line with an arrow and number 3, how that is -- as marked, how that is below what is marked as number 2 and that is marked, as the witness said, Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When you come there to that spot, then it's very clear. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are relying on the testimony of this witness in your report. You're not saying: I inspected the place myself and I know exactly where the dotted line should have been. That's -- you say: Mr. Djozo said this. And I have difficulties in finding that on this marked photograph. And if you could assist me in -- not by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I visited the place myself and I understand why it's difficult for you to see it in the photograph. The photograph was taken from a big distance and this is a projection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are relying on the testimony of a witness in a certain context, and what you are now telling us is that it's not that much that you relied on that witness but, rather, on your own observation. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm only trying to clear up the situation. I visited the place, and in the context of his testimony, I recognised the place. I don't know if I can find a photograph here where it's more clearly visible taken from Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to incident F-16 in this indictment, which is F-17 at your report, at the section beginning at English page 239, B/C/S page -- oh, I think I might have the wrong page number. English page 247, paragraphs 236 to 246. And that's this -- one of the sniping incidents from -- alleged sniping incidents from Spicasta Stijena. Now, between your report and your testimony, you make two assertions -- in fact, you make two identical assertions with respect to this incident that you did in your Karadzic report. And the first is, effectively, that when the victim of this shooting, Tarik Zunic, testified and identified the location where he was hit by gun-fire on March 6th, 1995, he identified the wrong spot. That's one of them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I explained why.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, yeah. What you did was you explained it's your view -- you told us in your report that it's your view he identified the wrong spot and you formed that view on the basis of information you received from a couple who you happened upon who lived down the street; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this couple told you that it actually happened in front of their house instead of where the victim said it happened; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you don't have any names or contact details of this couple; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to explain the context, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First answer the question, please, whether you have any contact details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have these details. I know where they are and I can contact them, though. But for certain reasons, I didn't take their contact details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the man offered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What were those reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll explain. When we were touring these locations in Sarajevo, had a meeting at the agency of Bosnia-Herzegovina called SIPA. And the director of SIPA recommended, for security reasons, that we do not tell people that we were experts for the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic and to say instead only that we were from the Hague Tribunal. We had police escort. And when we came to that location, I told the driver -- upon recognising the spot that Tarik Zunic identified as the place of the incident, there is a house there with a distinctive roof, and the police car was already 15 metres ahead of us. They were already in the street, and a man motioned to me: Come here, come here. I came up to the man and then he explained to me that he was an eye-witness of that incident and that he personally helped UNPROFOR personnel to put Tarik Zunic in a vehicle. And he described the incident in a way which is very consistent with the reports of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you go far beyond my question. You've answered my question. The reason is that you were -- you didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just didn't answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, I mean, I did understand your answer to be that you did not present yourself as investigating for the Karadzic Defence, and that for that reason you just did not enter into further details with them. But if I'm wrong, then please, instead of telling us all kind of other things, tell us then exactly why you didn't take the details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are completely right. The man offered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I thanked him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what was the distance exactly between the one spot and the other which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my rough estimate it's about 15 metres. For instance, on this photograph 181 where Tarik Zunic marked his position -- excuse me. The place that I was shown was 2 or 3 metres from this lamp-post, so the difference is about 15 metres, I think. These buildings are almost identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said that you believed them better than Mr. Zunic himself. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I explained why. Because people described the incident in the same way as described in UNPROFOR documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now did Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Tarik Zunic was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did Mr. Zunic describe the incident in a different way from what is found in the report? Or was his description of the event also consistent with what we find in the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report or the UNPROFOR report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: UNPROFOR report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His testimony is a little different. He only says that he heard two shots from an M84 machine-gun, and he says he was lying on the ground until the UNPROFOR came. One should bear in mind that he was on his way from school and it's possible that he didn't know what had happened before or after. He says he was lying on the ground and the man that I mentioned before said the same. They were unable to put him in a car immediately because there was shooting. Tarik Zunic does not mention that. At least not that I could find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not inconsistent with what UNPROFOR reported? I mean, if he's silent on a certain matter it doesn't mean that he disagrees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I'm saying that perhaps time intervals do not coincide with what UNPROFOR reports for that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps. Because I'm trying to understand. You say I have two narratives of the event: One by Mr. -- the victim himself and the other by a neighbour. And then you say: Since what the neighbour tells us is not inconsistent with and is rather consistent with the UNPROFOR report, that's why I believe him. At the same time when I ask you is then the Zunic narrative, is that inconsistent with UNPROFOR, you say: No, it's not inconsistent. So therefore, why do you choose for the one which is not inconsistent and why do you not choose for the other which is not inconsistent? I'm trying to understand your choice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here is why: Because this man lives in that house, he still lives there today, so he has immediate knowledge. Tarik Zunic was just passing by that house when he was wounded. When he was wounded, he probably didn't give any thought to remembering that house. Those houses are very similar, and it's completely possible in my mind that he believes it was by the house next door. He could be wrong about the appearance of the house, but this man lives there and he had a better opportunity to view the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how you weigh the statements, one by the victim himself who, if I understand well, passed every day on his way to school and perhaps back, and an unknown person who lived there. You say he knows the area, therefore he is to be believed. That is your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my conclusion, but it's up to you to make yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this got anything to do with your field of expertise? To believe A and not believe B because they are living there or passing by, whatever, is that in any way related to your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't fall within my field. It just concerns the place of incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please -- you've answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are two pieces information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the location the victim identified -- the specific location identified and marked by the victim has a clear and unobstructed line of sight to Spicasta Stijena; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the one you chose doesn't; right? That's the difference --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- between the two of them. The --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That place too is visible from Spicasta Stijena --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- just a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Look at your own report and I'll read you the very last sentence of paragraph 242. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In B/C/S I think it would be the immediately preceding page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it it's the last line above 181 -- image 181.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, in English you have to go back over to the succeeding page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we went on the wrong version to the page. One page back in B/C/S and one page forward into -- in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the difference is that the location you chose when you rejected testimony under oath and adopted the narrative of the people you met on the street was to move the incident location from a place that had a clear and unobstructed line of sight to Spicasta Stijena to a location that's much less visible, in your own words, than the location identified by the victim. That's the effect of what you did; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's exactly what the witness said today on the transcript. If we read the transcript. It's line 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although Ms. Edgerton tried three times to interrupt the witness what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at what the witness exactly said. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it's from lines 3 to 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. The first question was whether the location identified by the victim was -- had a clear and unobstructed line of sight to Spicasta Stijena. The witness confirmed that. And then the question was put to the witness: "And the one you chose doesn't; right? That's the difference." And then the answer was: "No." Between the two of them, as a matter of fact, here the witness interrupts Ms. Edgerton, as far as I can see, but at least the answer is "no." And the issue therefore was whether there was a clear and unobstructed line of sight. And did you want to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And then the witness said: "That place too is visible from Spicasta Stijena, just a little bit less."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's, Ms. Edgerton, an analysis to say that the clear and unobstructed line was not confirmed, but that there was visibility but a little bit less was confirmed by the witness. And that's what is found in his report and that seems to be consistent with the testimony he gave a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The difference is in the report it says "it is much less visible," and in his testimony today "it is a little bit less visible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's not exactly the same. There is a detail there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, your second -- sort of the main crux of one of your other arguments is that you say, effectively, that the victim here was shot in an exchange of fire; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't draw that conclusion on the basis of his ability, if that's what you're referring to. I did it on the basis of medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What you do is you assert he was shot in an exchange of fire and you cite in your footnote 469 to an UNPROFOR report for this day, and that report is now P674, as evidence in support of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Ms. Edgerton, could I ask one question. You -- earlier we had a look at the location as marked by Tarik Zunic and there was a photograph in which apparently you were measuring the vegetation. When was that photograph taken? That's number 182.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was taken on the day of the on-site investigation, September 2010. That's when we measured -- measured the road below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's 15 years after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I think it's time for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore let's not proceed but let's take a break. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, I briefly deal with a similar matter, that is the replacement of English translation of Exhibit D588. This exhibit was admitted on the 22nd of July, 2014. On the 7th of April of this year, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence that several pages were missing from the English translation but that a full translation had now been uploaded into e-court under 65 ter number 30998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence advised the Chamber that it would inform the Chamber that same day on whether it objects to the new English translation. To this day, the Chamber has not heard from the Defence. The Chamber therefore instructs the Registry to replace the previous English translation with the corrected version uploaded under 65 ter number 30998, and gives the Defence one week from today to revisit the matter. Mr. Poparic, similar apologies but we'll now proceed. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, yes, just before I begin, those pages of the testimony in the Karadzic trial of Mr. Nedzib Djozo have been uploaded under 65 ter number 33368, and P7596 was the exhibit number that's been reserved for those. So may those please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7596, which is now a two-page excerpt of testimony in the Karadzic case by Mr. Nedzib Djozo, is hereby admitted into evidence. And, Madam Registrar, the 65 ter number is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 33368 [Realtime transcript read in error "3368"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Poparic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is still one 3 missing. It should be 65 ter 33368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that, Madam Registrar, the number you mentioned, which is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are. And that document is now admitted as P7596. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poparic, when you talked about this incident in the Karadzic trial, you said that all the facts -- to use your own words: All the facts point to a conclusion that the victim was walking home from school through a substantial exchange of fire and shot as a result, and that UNPROFOR reports and other documents testified to that. And that was at transcript page 38925 to -26, and it's found in e-court page -- 65 ter number 32787, e-court pages 55 and 56. Now, you've abandoned that argument, haven't you, because there is no evidence that there was an exchange of fire going on at all; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day there was an exchange of gun-fire. There is no denying that. A major exchange. I don't know whether it happened at that particular moment, though. Assumption is that that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The only exchange -- or the only firing, because there is no mention of an exchange, the only firing that was going on that day in the documents you cite at footnotes 468 and 469 of your report are -- is firing -- actually is direct, deliberate targeting by SRK forces on Spicasta Stijena of civilians and UN personnel who were trying to help sniping victims. Is that what you're describing as an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where can we find this? Because my learned friend already called P674. It's not what we can find in that document. Maybe somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if she can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any dispute about what is found in those footnotes, Ms. Edgerton, you are invited to show it to us and to tell us what is there not consistent with what the report tells us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. Let's have a look, please, at P674.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's a document that you cited in your Karadzic report and in this report at, as I said, footnote 469.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go over and have a look at paragraph 4c of this document, which is on page 2 of both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. At the very top of the English page and about one-third of the way down in the B/C/S page, you see the report of eight explosions, seven machine-gun bursts, and 93 rounds of small arms fire. And then you see the asterisk after the mention of the small arms fire that refers to page 3a of this same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go over back to page -- paragraph 3a. Can we go over back to paragraph 3a. It's on page 1 in both languages. So 3a specifically says: "While assisting casualties reported at paragraphs 8.a.ii and a.iii, UNMOs came under occasional small arms fire. Number of rounds unknown but origin of fire assessed as being Spicasta Stijena ..." Now, do you want to go to 3b?
